--- title: "Creating a Metacheck Report" vignette: > %\VignetteIndexEntry{Creating a Metacheck Report} %\VignetteEngine{knitr::rmarkdown} %\VignetteEncoding{UTF-8} --- So far we have looked at individual modules in isolation. In practice you usually want to run *several* checks on a paper at once and collect the results into a single document you can read, save, or hand to a co-author. This chapter shows how to go from a single paper object to a full Metacheck report. We start with the all-in-one `report()` function, and its counterpart `report_repository()` for when you have a folder of shared files rather than a manuscript. We then unpack what they do — running one module with `module_run()`, running several with `report_module_run()`, and turning the result into a document with `report_qmd()`. Finally we cover the slightly tricky part: passing settings through to the modules. ## Loading a paper Every report starts from a **paper object**, created with `read()` (see [Reading in a Paper](reading-a-paper.qmd)). Throughout this chapter we use the bundled demo paper, which `demopaper()` returns directly so the examples run without a network connection: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paper <- demopaper() paper$paper_id ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "to_err_is_human" ``` ::: ::: In your own work you would instead read a converted file: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paper <- read("converted/my_manuscript.json") ``` ::: Everything below works on this single `paper` object. The same functions also accept a *paperlist* (a list of papers), so the same code scales to a whole corpus — see [Batch processing](reading-a-paper.qmd) and [Using the Paper Database Corpora](papers-databases.qmd). ## The quick way: `report()` `report()` runs a set of modules on a paper and writes a finished report to disk. With no other arguments it runs the **default battery** of fifteen modules and saves an HTML file named after the paper. The defaults span the whole manuscript: preregistration ([`prereg_check`](mod-prereg-check.qmd)), funding and conflict-of-interest statements ([`funding_check`](mod-funding-check.qmd), [`coi_check`](mod-coi-check.qmd)), statistical power ([`power`](mod-power.qmd)), data and code availability ([`repo_check`](mod-repo-check.qmd), [`code_check`](mod-code-check.qmd)), the reporting of statistics ([`stat_check`](mod-stat-check.qmd), [`stat_p_exact`](mod-stat-p-exact.qmd), [`stat_p_nonsig`](mod-stat-p-nonsig.qmd), [`stat_effect_size`](mod-stat-effect-size.qmd), [`marginal`](mod-marginal.qmd)), and the reference list ([`ref_replication`](mod-ref-replication.qmd), [`ref_retraction`](mod-ref-retraction.qmd), [`ref_pubpeer`](mod-ref-pubpeer.qmd), [`ref_summary`](mod-ref-summary.qmd)). [`ref_accuracy`](mod-ref-accuracy.qmd) is, for now, not among the defaults, because most of the references it flags turn out to be errors in reading the PDF; you can still add it to `modules` yourself. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report(paper) ``` ::: By default the report is saved as `"_report.html"` in the working directory; set `output_file` to choose your own name and location. The function returns the output of the modules, without printing it, and the path of the file it wrote is stored with that output: `attr(result, "save_path")`. For a list of papers, `report()` writes one report per paper, named `"_"`, and `save_path` holds one path per paper. Papers in a list that share a `paper_id` are first renamed `"~2"`, `"~3"`, and so on, with a warning, so that each gets its own report. ### Choosing modules You rarely need all the default checks. Pass a `modules` vector to run exactly the ones you want, in the order you want them reported: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report(paper, modules = c("stat_p_exact", "stat_p_nonsig", "marginal")) ``` ::: Use `module_list()` to see every built-in module, or `module_help("module_name")` for the details of one. A custom module is also given by name when you installed it with `module_install()`, or saved it as an `.R` file in your working directory or in a `modules/` folder there; any other custom module is given by its file path (see [Creating Modules](creating-modules.qmd)). ### Choosing the output format `report()` can write either a rendered **HTML** file or the intermediate **Quarto** source (`qmd`). The `qmd` option is useful when you want to edit the report before rendering, or render it yourself with different options: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report(paper, modules = c("stat_p_exact", "marginal"), output_file = "demo_report.html", output_format = "html") # the default report(paper, output_file = "demo_report.qmd", output_format = "qmd") # write the Quarto source instead ``` ::: Rendering to HTML requires [Quarto](https://quarto.org) to be installed. If rendering fails for any reason, `report()` falls back to saving the source (and warns you): the `qmd` file, or an R Markdown (`.Rmd`) file for the static report types `"simple"`, `"simple_brief"` and `"checklist"` (see below). So you never lose the result of running the modules. ### Choosing the report type `report_type` sets how the report is laid out and how much it contains: | `report_type` | What you get | |---|---| | `"full"` (default) | the interactive report: a light and dark theme, tables you can sort and page through, and tabbed sections | | `"brief"` | the same report, but only the modules with a red, yellow or failed light, each with its one-line summary | | `"simple"` | a static report without JavaScript: plain tables and headings in place of tabs. Use it for a report you will send by e-mail, since mail programs often flag the JavaScript in a full report | | `"simple_brief"` | the static layout of `"simple"` with the content of `"brief"` | | `"checklist"` | a static report laid out by check instead of by module (see below) | ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report(paper, report_type = "checklist") ``` ::: The **checklist** report sorts every check of every module into six groups: to fix, to improve, decide by hand, for information, fine, and not applicable, with the number in each group except "for information" at the top. Each check that needs work is a block that says what was found and what to do on separate lines, with its tables folded underneath. The checks that are fine or not applicable take one line each, and the explanation of how each module works is folded at the bottom. When [reproducibility_check](mod-reproducibility-check.qmd) ran the code, it gets a section of its own after the results: it says how the scripts were run and how many ran to the end, lists in run order what happened to each script (ran to the end, stopped with an error, with the error itself, ran out of time, could not run because a package is missing, or was not run, with the reason), names other problems in the files such as `setwd()` calls, and says how many of the statistical tests reported in the paper were found in the output of the code. The report uses the colours and font of [Metacheck's website on SURF Research Cloud](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/). How a module tells the checklist report what its checks are is explained in [Creating Modules](creating-modules.qmd). A module can ask to stay in the brief report whatever its light. [reproducibility_check](mod-reproducibility-check.qmd) does this when it ran at least one script, so that a successful run is not left out and the report does not read as if the code was never checked. ## Checking a folder instead of a paper: `report_repository()` Everything above starts from a manuscript. Sometimes there is no manuscript: you have a folder of shared files on your own computer — a repository you downloaded, or your own work before you share it — and you want to know what is in it and what could be improved. `report_repository()` is for that case. Give it a folder and it writes a report: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report_repository("my_downloaded_project") ``` ::: It runs the four modules that read a repository's files, in the order they depend on each other: | Module | What it asks | |---|---| | [`repo_check`](mod-repo-check.qmd) | What files are here? It sorts each into a type, looks inside `.zip` archives, and flags a missing README or an unreadable format. | | [`code_check`](mod-code-check.qmd) | What does the analysis code look like? Which language, which packages, does it parse, does it hard-code a path that only existed on one machine. | | [`data_check`](mod-data-check.qmd) | What is in the data? It describes every column and runs [data-quality checks](mod-data-validate.qmd), including a screen for columns that may hold personal information. | | [`codebook_check`](mod-codebook-check.qmd) | Are those columns documented anywhere? | The report is named after the folder, so the call above writes `my_downloaded_project_report.html` into your working directory. Name the file yourself to put it elsewhere, and pass `modules` to run fewer of them: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report_repository("my_downloaded_project", output_file = "reports/project_check.html") report_repository("my_downloaded_project", modules = c("repo_check", "data_check")) ``` ::: Only the folder you name is read. No links are followed and nothing is downloaded, so the whole thing works offline. Whether a language model is used follows your own `llm_use()` setting, exactly as when you run the modules individually. ::: {.callout-note} ## Without R [Metacheck's website](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/) checks a folder too: under *Run Metacheck on a Repository*, choose a folder or a .zip file, or paste a link to an online repository. It runs `repo_check`, `code_check`, and `data_check` (not `codebook_check`), can also run the R and Python code ([Reproducibility Check](mod-reproducibility-check.qmd)), and gives the brief report; the [ResearchBox Check](https://metacheckserve.metacheck.src.surf-hosted.nl/researchbox/) gives the checklist report. A folder you choose is uploaded to the server; the [Docker installation](get-started.qmd#docker-installation) offers the same website on your own computer. ::: ::: {.callout-note} ## Why you do not pass a paper The modules attach their results to a paper object, so `report_repository()` creates an empty one for them with `test_paper()`. You never see it, but it is why the report's header carries the folder name as its subtitle and lists no authors or DOI — there is no manuscript to take them from. If you *do* have the manuscript, read it with `read()` and use `report()` instead, and the repository modules will follow the links in the paper rather than needing a local folder. ::: ## Running a single module `report()` is convenient, but it always writes a file. While you are exploring a paper interactively it is often handier to run one module and look at the result in the console. That is what `module_run()` does: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mo <- module_run(paper, "stat_p_exact") ``` ::: The object it returns holds everything the module found. The pieces you will use most are the traffic light, the one-line summary, and the full results table: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mo$traffic_light ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "red" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} mo$summary_text ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 3 detected *p* values." ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} object gives a compact summary, and `module_report()` formats the same output as the Markdown section that would appear in a report: ```{.r .cell-code} module_report(mo) |> cat() ``` ### ⚠️ Exact P-Values {#exact-p-values .red} We found 1 imprecise *p* value out of 3 detected *p* values.
View detailed feedback Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "p > .05", Text = "There was no effect of experience on the reduction in errors when using the tool (p > .05), as the correlation was non-significant (Figure 2)."), row.names = c(NA, -1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame")) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association. :::
::: {.callout-note title="How It Works" collapse="true"} List any p-values reported with insufficient precision (e.g., p < .05 or p = n.s.) or reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000). This module uses regular expressions to identify p-values. It will flag any values reported as p > ? or p < numbers greater than .001. It will also flag p-values reported as exactly zero (e.g., p = .000, p = 0.00), which are mathematically impossible — p-values are never exactly zero and should instead be reported as p < .001. We try to exclude figure and table notes like "* p < .05", but may not succeed at excluding all false positives. This module only checks p-values reported in the running text of the manuscript. It cannot (yet) process p-values reported only in tables (as opposed to a table's footnote text, which the module does see and tries to exclude — see above). This module was developed by Lisa DeBruine and Daniel Lakens Read more in the [metacheck manual](https://www.scienceverse.org/metacheck_book/chapters/mod-stat-p-exact.html). ::: ::: {.validation} Validation: In a sample of 225 papers containing 405 instances of non-exact p-values, the module correctly detected 269 cases (true positives) and incorrectly identified 78 (false positives). It missed 136 instances of imprecisely reported p-values (false negatives) and correctly identified 4557 cases of precisely reported p-values (true negative). Additionally, 78% of positive detections were correct (positive predictive value). ::: ## Running multiple modules To run several modules and keep their combined output *without* writing a file, use `report_module_run()`. It takes the same `modules` vector as `report()` and returns a list of module outputs: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} module_output <- report_module_run( paper, modules = c("stat_p_exact", "stat_p_nonsig", "marginal") ) ``` ::: The result is a named list — one entry per module — that you can inspect individually: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} names(module_output) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "stat_p_exact" "stat_p_nonsig" "marginal" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} module_output[["marginal"]]$traffic_light ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "red" ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} module_output[["marginal"]]$summary_text ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> [1] "You described 2 effects with terms related to 'marginally significant'." ``` ::: ::: This is the same intermediate object `report()` builds internally. To turn it into a finished document yourself, pass it to `report_qmd()`, which produces the Quarto report text (header, summary section, and one section per module): ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report_text <- report_qmd(module_output, paper) writeLines(report_text, "demo_report.qmd") ``` ::: Splitting the work this way — run the modules once with `report_module_run()`, then format with `report_qmd()` — is useful when the modules are slow (for example reference checks that query external services) and you want to render the report more than once without re-running them. ## Passing settings to modules This is the part that trips people up. Some modules take **extra arguments** beyond `paper`. For example: - `power(paper, seed = 8675309)` — the random seed used when sampling text for the LLM. - `ref_replication(paper, show_outcomes = FALSE)` — whether to include replication outcomes. - `repo_check(paper, local_path = NULL, local_only = FALSE)` — where to find the repository, and whether to skip online lookups. `module_help("module_name")` shows the arguments a given module accepts: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} module_help("power") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #> Power Analysis Check #> #> This module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. If specified by the user, it also uses a large language model (LLM) to extract information reported in power analyses, including the statistical test, sample size, alpha level, desired level of power, and magnitude and type of effect size. #> #> module_run(paper, "power", seed = 8675309) #> #> - paper: a paper object or paperlist object #> - seed: a seed for the LLM #> #> The Power Analysis Check module uses regular expressions to identify sentences that contain a statistical power analysis. Without the use of an LLM, the module uses regular expressions to classify the power analysis as a-priori, sensitivity or post-hoc. With the use of an LLM, it checks if the power analysis is reported with all required information. #> #> The regular expressions can miss power analyses, or fail to classify them correctly. The type of power analysis is often difficult to classify, which can easily be solved by explicitly specifying the type of power analysis as 'a-priori', 'sensitivity', or 'post-hoc'. Note that 'post-hoc' or 'observed' power is rarely useful. The LLM can fail to identify information in the paper, and will not have access to information in paragraphs in the paper other than those that contain the word 'power'. This package was validated by the Metacheck team on articles in Psychological Science. #> #> In a sample of 128 papers with 246 instances of power statements, 203 were correctly detected (true positives), 22 were missed (false negatives) and 21 were incorrectly detected (false positives). Overall, among all instances flagged as power statements, 90.6% were correct (positive predictive value). ``` ::: ::: How you supply these arguments depends on which function you are using. ### One module: pass arguments directly With `module_run()`, extra arguments go straight through the `...`, exactly as if you were calling the module function itself: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} module_run(paper, "power", seed = 123) module_run(paper, "ref_replication", show_outcomes = TRUE) ``` ::: ### Several modules: the `args` list When you run *several* modules at once with `report()` or `report_module_run()`, you cannot use `...`, because an argument like `seed` would be ambiguous — which module is it for? Instead you pass a single `args` argument: **a named list of lists**, where each name matches a module name and each value is the list of arguments for that module. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} args <- list( power = list(seed = 123), ref_replication = list(show_outcomes = TRUE), repo_check = list(local_only = TRUE) ) report_module_run( paper, modules = c("power", "ref_replication", "repo_check"), args = args ) ``` ::: The same `args` list works with `report()`: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report( paper, modules = c("power", "ref_replication", "repo_check"), args = args ) ``` ::: A few rules make this easier to get right: - **You only list the modules that need arguments.** Modules you do not mention in `args` run with their defaults, even if they are in `modules`. So a module taking no special settings (like `stat_p_exact`) never needs an entry. - **The names must match the module names** in your `modules` vector. A mismatched name (a typo, or a module not actually being run) is silently ignored — its settings simply have no effect. - **Each value is itself a list**, even when there is a single argument: `power = list(seed = 123)`, not `power = 123`. Putting it together, here is a complete report that runs four modules, two of them with custom settings and two with their defaults: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} report( paper, modules = c("stat_p_exact", "marginal", "power", "ref_replication"), args = list( power = list(seed = 123), ref_replication = list(show_outcomes = TRUE) ), output_file = "demo_report.html" ) ``` ::: ## Summary | You want to… | Use | |---|---| | Run modules and write a finished report file | `report(paper, modules, output_file, output_format, report_type, args)` | | Check a folder of files, with no manuscript | `report_repository(path, output_file, output_format, report_type, modules, args)` | | Run one module and inspect the result | `module_run(paper, module, ...)` | | Run several modules, keep the result, write no file | `report_module_run(paper, modules, args)` | | Format module output as report text | `report_qmd(module_output, paper)` or `module_report(mo)` | | Pass settings to one module | extra arguments to `module_run()` | | Pass settings to several modules | the `args` named-list-of-lists |
